slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Circle and chords: groups count regions for 1 to 5 points, predict 6, then count carefully (no three chords meeting at one inside point). The 31 surprise starts the lesson.

  • I can make a conjecture from a pattern and test it.
  • I can build a second rule that fits the same data, to show that a pattern is not a proof.
  • I can use one counterexample to show a conjecture is false.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A pattern can give you a good guess, called a conjecture. Checking only some cases does not by itself prove a claim beyond those cases. If a claim is restricted to a stated finite set, checking every member exactly can prove it for that set. One valid counterexample in the claimed domain refutes a universal claim. (In plain words: Checking some cases by itself does not prove a claim about cases you have not checked. If the claim is only about a stated finite list and you check every item exactly, that proves it for that list. One actual counterexample from the claimed domain disproves a "for every" claim.)

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• inductive reasoning Spotting a pattern in examples and guessing it always holds.
  • conjecture A guess based on a pattern that has not been proved yet.
  • counterexample One example that makes a statement false.
  • for every Means the statement must work in all cases, not just most.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Do three values pin down a rule?

Read the worked steps
StepReason
For n = 0, 1, 2 the values are 1, 3, 5. The rule f(n) = 2n + 1 fits.Plug in: 1, 3, 5. It fits all three.
Now try a second rule: g(n) = 2n + 1 + n(n - 1)(n - 2).We added a piece that is zero for n = 0, 1 and 2.
At n = 0, 1 or 2, one of n, n - 1 or n - 2 is zero, so the extra piece is 0. So g also gives 1, 3, 5.Anything times zero is zero.
At n = 3: f(3) = 7, but g(3) = 7 + 3 · 2 · 1 = 13.Now no factor is zero.
Two rules fit the data but disagree at n = 3. So three values do not prove f(n) = 2n + 1.A proof needs a reason that covers every n.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Build a second rule that fits.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
For n = 0, 1, 2 the values are 2, 5, 10. Someone guesses n² + 2n + 2.Plug in: 2, 5, 10. It fits.
Add the zero-maker piece: g(n) = n² + 2n + 2 + n(n - 1)(n - 2).This piece is 0 at n = 0, 1 and 2.
So g also gives 2, 5, 10.Same values where we have data.
At n = 3 the guess gives 17, and g gives 17 + 6 = 23.3 · 2 · 1 = 6.
Two different rules match the data. The data alone can't choose between them.A short list does not fix the next value.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Kai counts circle regions for 1 to 5 points: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Kai writes 'It doubles, so 6 points give 32.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A pattern is only a guess. Count carefully, with no three chords through one inside point. There are 31 regions, so 'it doubles' is false.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
For n = 0, 1, 2 the values are 1, 3, 5. Does that prove f(n) = 2n + 1 for every whole number n? Compare two rules at n = 5.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. g(n) = 2n + 1 + n(n - 1)(n - 2) also fits 1, 3, 5. At n = 5, f(5) = 11 but g(5) = 71. Two rules fit, so the data don't prove either one.

Reveal second check

At n = 0, 1, 2 the extra piece has a zero factor. At n = 5 none of its factors is zero, so the rules split.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Ana checks a rule on 100 examples and it works every time. Ben finds one example where it fails, and his example is correct. Who settles the question, and which way?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Ben does. One correct counterexample proves the rule is false. 100 examples that work can't prove it for every case.

Reveal second check

'Not every x works' means 'at least one x fails.' Ben's example is exactly that.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
A rule is claimed only for the numbers 1, 2 and 3. All three were checked carefully. Is that a proof for those three numbers? Is it a proof for every positive whole number?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Yes for {1, 2, 3}: every number in that list was checked. No for all positive whole numbers: other numbers were never checked.

Reveal second check

Nothing in {1, 2, 3} is left out. But 4 is a positive whole number that nobody checked.
